title: RLDiscover: LLM-Driven Co-Evolutionof Reinforcement Learning Algorithms

paper.title: RLDiscover: LLM-Driven Co-Evolution of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms
paper.abstract:
Abstract LLM-guided program evolution has enabled discoveries in mathematics
and computational optimization, raising the prospect of reinforcement
learning (RL) algorithms that self-evolve to improve how agents learn.
However, realizing this prospect faces two obstacles. Joint search over coupled
algorithmic components is difficult to scale: simultaneous changes
can disrupt learning, while isolated changes overlook their
dependencies. Evaluating candidate algorithms also requires costly
training, with fitness remaining uncertain across random seeds.
We introduce RLDiscover, a framework for the self-evolution of model-free
deep RL algorithms. Progressive Co-Evolution advances from targeted
component edits to joint evolution, while Progressive Probabilistic
Evaluation balances search breadth and evaluation fidelity through
staged training and repeated evaluation. Experiments across SAC,
PPO, and DQN on four benchmark suites show substantial improvements
in mean return, with per-family median gains of 32 % 32\% – 84 % 84\% and a peak return ratio of approximately 363 × 363\times over a near-zero
baseline. These gains include transitions from failed learning to
successful task completion, and improvements persist when evolution
starts from stronger open-source implementations. On measured SAC
locomotion runs, evaluation uses approximately one-fifteenth the
estimated compute required to fully evaluate the same candidate pool.
Remarkably, independent searches repeatedly discover interpretable combinations
of adaptive robust losses, progress-dependent value targets, and
running statistics, with selected programs transferring to unseen
tasks. These findings point toward a broader role for self-evolution
in AI: discovering interpretable algorithms that improve how agents learn. 1 1 1 Code and data will be publicly released upon acceptance.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: arXiv.org perpetual non-exclusive license arXiv:2610.09218v1 [cs.AI] 06 Oct 2026 RLDiscover: LLM-Driven Co-Evolution of Reinforcement Learning Algorithms Haoran Li, Zengle Ge, Xiaomin Yuan, YUI LO, Songlin Zhou, Jiahua Ying, Haoxin Li, Qianhui Liu, Yuanhang Liu, Jiaqun Liu, GUOKAI CHEN, Mingju Chen, Ruinan Wang, Annan Li, Jianmin Wu, Dawei Yin, Dou Shen University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences Baidu Tsinghua University Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Peking University Shanghai University University of Bristol Abstract LLM-guided program evolution has enabled discoveries in mathematics and computational optimization, raising the prospect of reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms that self-evolve to improve how agents learn. However, realizing this prospect faces two obstacles. Joint search over coupled algorithmic components is difficult to scale: simultaneous changes can disrupt learning, while isolated changes overlook their dependencies. Evaluating candidate algorithms also requires costly training, with fitness remaining uncertain across random seeds. We introduce RLDiscover, a framework for the self-evolution of model-free deep RL algorithms. Progressive Co-Evolution advances from targeted component edits to joint evolution, while Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation balances search breadth and evaluation fidelity through staged training and repeated evaluation. Experiments across SAC, PPO, and DQN on four benchmark suites show substantial improvements in mean return, with per-family median gains of 32 % 32\% – 84 % 84\% and a peak return ratio of approximately 363 × 363\times over a near-zero baseline. These gains include transitions from failed learning to successful task completion, and improvements persist when evolution starts from stronger open-source implementations. On measured SAC locomotion runs, evaluation uses approximately one-fifteenth the estimated compute required to fully evaluate the same candidate pool. Remarkably, independent searches repeatedly discover interpretable combinations of adaptive robust losses, progress-dependent value targets, and running statistics, with selected programs transferring to unseen tasks. These findings point toward a broader role for self-evolution in AI: discovering interpretable algorithms that improve how agents learn. 1 1 1 Code and data will be publicly released upon acceptance. 1 Introduction LLM-guided program evolution makes executable algorithmic logic a direct object of search: language models propose code changes, and evaluation feedback guides their selection ( Lehman et al., 2022 ) . FunSearch demonstrated the potential of this approach for mathematical discovery ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ) ; AlphaEvolve extended it to larger programs and computational optimization tasks ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) ; and ShinkaEvolve developed mechanisms for more sample-efficient program evolution ( Lange et al., 2025 ) . These advances motivate applying program evolution to the learning procedures that govern how artificial agents improve through experience. Reinforcement learning (RL) offers a natural target: an RL algorithm is itself a program specifying how experience is transformed into updates to an agent’s predictions and behavior Oh et al. (2020) . We focus on model-free deep RL, encompassing value-based methods such as DQN ( Mnih et al., 2015 ) , actor-critic methods such as PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) , and SAC ( Haarnoja et al., 2018 ) . These algorithms specify how experience is converted into learning targets, value estimates, and policy updates. Their implementations therefore offer a structured space for discovering improvements to how agents learn. However, evolving interacting components of deep RL algorithms faces two difficulties. First, joint search over coupled components is difficult to scale . Broad randomization often yields little learning, while the same design change can have opposite effects: increasing data reuse can help PPO but hurt vanilla policy gradients ( Andrychowicz et al., 2021 ) . These observations show that broad simultaneous changes can disrupt learning, while optimizing choices in a fixed context can overlook their dependencies. Second, candidate fitness is expensive and imperfectly observed . In our experiments, fully evaluating 230 candidate programs would cost approximately 1330 GPU-hours per search run (Appendix J , Table 8 ). 2 2 2 The evaluation strategy introduced below uses approximately 87 GPU-hours for this candidate volume, a 15.3 × 15.3\times reduction relative to the estimated full-evaluation cost. Moreover, full-length training does not eliminate uncertainty caused by random seeds: On mw-pick-place-v3 , the same evolved program obtains returns of 2.9, 2887.3, and 3.9 across three seeds (Appendix K ). These observations expose competing demands on the evaluation budget: exploring many programs requires inexpensive feedback, while determining whether apparent improvements persist requires more extensive, repeated training. This motivates RLDiscover, a framework that addresses these challenges through structured proposals and staged evaluation. Its search space consists of five algorithmic components within a working RL implementation. 3 3 3 The interfaces cover common RL computations: observation processing, target/advantage estimation, value-function losses, policy objectives, and reward processing with exploration bonuses ( Bou et al., 2023 ; Burda et al., 2019 ) . Their use is trainer-dependent. Appendix D gives the full interface specifications. Progressive Co-Evolution (PCE) first allocates mutations among individual components using a UCB-inspired rule, then permits joint revisions across components, allowing the search to build on targeted changes while exploring their interactions. Progressive Probabilistic Evaluation (PPE) allocates training compute through increasingly demanding evaluations, reserving full training for a small set of finalists. Together, they implement a simple design principle: structure the search to generate useful candidates, and increase evaluation effort as the candidate pool is narrowed. We instantiate the framework on SAC, PPO, and DQN, covering off-policy and on-policy learning as well as continuous and discrete control. Our contributions are: 1. Efficient RL algorithm evolution. We introduce PCE and PPE to address component dependencies and costly, noisy evaluations. On measured SAC locomotion runs, they reduce evaluation cost by approximately 15 × 15\times relative to evaluating the same number of candidates at full fidelity. 2. Broad improvements across algorithms and benchmarks. Across four benchmark suites, RLDiscover improves mean return on all 26 tested task–algorithm pairs spanning SAC, PPO, and DQN, with median gains of 39.8 % 39.8\% , 83.6 % 83.6\% , and 32.1 % 32.1\% , respectively. Improvements also persist when evolution starts from stronger open-source SAC implementations, with positive gains on all nine tested tasks. 3. Convergent discovery of interpretable mechanisms. Task-specific searches repeatedly recover shared mechanisms, including robust critic losses in 16/17 SAC and 5/5 PPO champions. Cross-task evaluations further demonstrate transfer of evolved programs to unseen tasks, showing that program evolution recovers reusable learning mechanisms beyond hyperparameter tuning. 2 Related Work Discovering RL algorithms. Prior work discovers learning objectives and update rules through evolutionary optimization and meta-learning. Evolved Policy Gradients ( Houthooft et al., 2018 ) and MetaGenRL ( Kirsch et al., 2020 ) learn parameterized objectives, while LPG ( Oh et al., 2020 ) and DiscoRL ( Oh et al., 2025 ) meta-learn neural update rules. AutoML-Zero and Evolving RL Algorithms search programs or computation graphs constructed from predefined operation libraries ( Real et al., 2020 ; Co-Reyes et al., 2021 ) . Eureka instead generates reward programs within an existing learning pipeline ( Ma et al., 2024 ) . A parallel line applies the same foundation-model code-evolution paradigm to adversarial multi-agent games, where the evaluation landscape shifts as strategies improve and reliable assessment therefore requires evaluator co-evolution and hierarchical evaluation ( Anonymous, 2026 ) . Our focus is source-code modification across multiple components of working RL implementations. Through fixed function interfaces, RLDiscover edits observation processing, targets, objectives, and reward shaping, and studies how to coordinate these modifications under a limited evaluation budget. Multi-fidelity evaluation and search allocation. Successive Halving ( Jamieson and Talwalkar, 2016 ) and Hyperband allocate ( Li et al., 2018 ) increasing resources to promising configurations; BOHB combines this allocation with model-guided candidate generation ( Falkner et al., 2018 ) . PPE applies staged evaluation to evolving RL programs to balance candidate coverage against the reliability of performance estimates. For proposal allocation, PCE uses a UCB-inspired rule to select components for mutation ( Auer et al., 2002 ) , before allowing joint program revisions. These mechanisms adapt established allocation ideas to the coupled search and evaluation of RL implementations. 3 Method Figure 1: RLDiscover overview. Left : 5 algorithm components of RL algorithms (state representation, value estimation, critic learning, policy optimization, exploration). Center : PCE evolves components independently (Phase 1, UCB1 selection), then co-evolves them jointly (Phase 2). Right : PPE filters candidates through L0 → \to L1 → \to L2, so only candidates that survive cheap screening consume a full-length training run. Top : the LLM mutation engine generates code variants guided by performance feedback. 3.1 Five-Component Decomposition Given a base RL algorithm, let 𝐦 = ( m 1 , … , m K ) \mathbf{m}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{K}) , with K = 5 K=5 , denote the implementations of its five algorithmic components.
